tldr: By integrating a pneumatic bending soft finger and a vision-based tactile sensor into a unified simulation environment using the Material Point Method (MPM) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), this work accomplishes delicate contact tasks on real hardware via calibration from minimal real images and simulation demonstration augmentation.
hero_caption: Overview of the PneuTac framework. MPM particles and 3DGS are jointly initialized from CAD models to faithfully reproduce soft robot bending, tactile gel deformation, and internal illumination in a unified manner. This enables demonstration augmentation in simulation and smooth transfer to delicate real-world contact tasks.
overview:
Soft pneumatic robots, which provide inherently compliant and safe interaction, paired with vision-based tactile sensors that capture contact surface details at high resolution, represent an ideal combination for delicate manipulation. However, training policies for this pairing with machine learning traditionally requires collecting massive amounts of real-world demonstrations on fragile soft parts, where hardware wear and data collection costs pose major bottlenecks.

While turning to simulation is an intuitive solution, existing tools typically isolate rigid robots with tactile sensors from tactile-free soft robots alone. None have provided an environment capable of accurately simulating both as an integrated system. Furthermore, calibrating simulation parameters for soft materials (real-to-sim identification) usually demands extensive data and tedious manual tuning.

To overcome these hurdles, the authors propose "PneuTac", a unified framework combining the Material Point Method (MPM)—known for robust handling of large deformations and contact—with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for fast, high-quality rendering. Using a simple vision-based calibration pipeline with just a few camera images, PneuTac reproduces the appearance and physical behavior of real hardware, accelerates computation by several orders of magnitude using surrogate models, and expands a small set of real demonstrations tenfold within simulation.

In experiments using a custom-built pneumatic soft finger with a tactile sensing tip, the framework achieved significantly higher success rates across three delicate real-world tasks—switch flipping, egg carton opening, and card pulling—compared to baselines trained on the same amount of real data. It offers a practical breakthrough that paves the way for compliant robot tactile Sim-to-Real transfer at realistic costs.
contributions: Developed "PneuTac", the first unified framework to jointly simulate the deformation and appearance of pneumatic soft actuators and vision-based tactile sensors using MPM and 3DGS.

Introduced a highly efficient real-to-sim calibration method that accurately estimates robot material parameters, pneumatic gains, and tactile sensor photometric properties from only a few static and indentation images.
Employed neural surrogate models to replace full MPM computation, achieving a 5x speedup for robot kinematics and an approximately 3000x acceleration for tactile rendering.

Implemented tactile-guided demonstration augmentation tracking both trajectory and tactile contact area in simulation, demonstrating substantial performance improvements on three contact-rich real-world tasks.

sections.heading: Why Couldn't Existing Simulators Handle Soft Robots with Tactile Sensing?
sections.summary: Tactile simulators have assumed rigid robot mountings, while soft robot simulators have ignored contact and tactile sensing. PneuTac closes this gap by combining deformable body physics with 3DGS rendering.
sections.details:
When attempting to simulate soft robot contact manipulation, researchers previously had to compromise between two divided fields.

### Vision-Based Tactile Sensor Simulation
Existing tactile simulators such as Taxim, DiffTactile, and Tacchi model gel deformation and light reflection, but they are all designed assuming sensors are mounted onto rigid robots. In addition, calibrating their rendering parameters requires large volumes of real contact data.

### Soft Robot Simulation
While extensive research uses finite element methods (FEM) or GPU physics engines to simulate soft robot motions, solving the non-linear dynamics of the compliant robot body alone is computationally demanding. Simulators capable of integrating delicate contact and full tactile sensor feedback for policy learning have been lacking.

### Coupling Physics with 3D Gaussians
Recent works like PhysGaussian and PhysTwin drive 3DGS Gaussian kernels directly with MPM particles. However, these frameworks have been restricted to passive deformable objects like cloth or ropes. PneuTac makes a decisive leap forward by applying this integration to actively driven pneumatic robots and tactile sensors for sim-to-real policy learning.

sections.heading: The Complete Pipeline: From MPM-3DGS Integration to Surrogate Acceleration
sections.summary: MPM particles and 3DGS are coupled from CAD models and aligned to real hardware using simple image-based calibration. Two neural networks dramatically accelerate computation, enabling tactile-guided demonstration augmentation in simulation.
sections.details:
The PneuTac pipeline comprises four key steps: unified simulation construction, image-based calibration, surrogate model acceleration, and tactile-guided demonstration collection.

### III-A MPM-3DGS Simulation
To capture the deformation dynamics of both the soft robot body and the tactile sensor gel, the framework adopts the Material Point Method (MPM), which reliably calculates large deformations and contact using a hybrid Eulerian-grid and Lagrangian-particle formulation. Sampled from CAD models, particles for pneumatic chamber bending are driven via an approximation based on a rigid multi-joint spine (Compatible Particle-in-Cell model). For appearance, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) binds Gaussian centers 1-to-1 with MPM particles. Internal color LED illumination in the tactile sensor is modeled using a contact photometric formulation $\mathbf{c}_g = \mathbf{c}^0_g + w_g [\mathbf{L}\nabla d_g + \mathbf{c}_d\bar{d}_g]$, which depends on gel surface gradient $\nabla d_g$ and indentation depth $\bar{d}_g$.

### III-B Vision-Based Real-to-Sim Modelling
Physical parameters are identified using standard camera images rather than complex external measurement devices. Parameters such as soft finger Young's modulus $E_s$ and pneumatic bending gain $G$ are optimized using CMA-ES against a combination of appearance loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{app}}$ and silhouette Intersection-over-Union (IoU) across static images under six pressure levels. Similarly, tactile sensor photometric coefficients are optimized from just a single uncompressed reference image and one indentation image with a known probe.

### III-C Acceleration via Action and Perception Networks
Because full MPM simulation is computationally heavy, two surrogate networks are introduced for policy learning. For robot kinematics, an MLP predicts residual joint torques $\boldsymbol{\tau}_r$ added to a simplified kinematic model. For tactile perception, a UNet maps deformation from a fast probe-grid model $\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\mathrm{probe}}$ to high-fidelity MPM surface deformation $\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\mathrm{mpm}}$.

### III-D Tactile-Guided Demonstration Collection
Using only 10 successful demonstrations collected on the real robot, demonstrations are augmented in simulation using GPU-parallelized Model Predictive Control (CEM-MPC). By incorporating both end-effector tracking and the evolution of contact pixel count (contact area ratio $c_t$) from tactile images into the cost function, 100 realistic demonstration trajectories with proper object contact are automatically synthesized.

sections.heading: Validation Across Three Delicate Real-World Manipulation Tasks
sections.summary: A custom tactile pneumatic soft finger mounted on a Panda robot was evaluated on switch flipping, egg carton opening, and card pulling. Policies trained via Behavior Cloning (BC) were evaluated after augmenting 10 real demos into 100 in simulation.
sections.details:
To rigorously evaluate the proposed method, extensive experiments spanning hardware fabrication to real-world task setups were conducted.

### Hardware Setup and Experimental Environment
A single-chamber pneumatic soft finger was fabricated on a Stratasys 3D printer by co-printing Agilus30 rubber-like material (flexible sections) and Vero rigid material (spine segments). A Digit vision-based tactile sensor equipped with an Ecoflex gel tip was mounted at the distal end, which was attached to a Franka Emika Panda arm. To assess generalizability, cross-device calibration experiments were also conducted on a distinct 3-chamber soft arm and an unmodified commercial Digit sensor. Computations were executed on a single NVIDIA RTX 5070 Ti GPU.

### Evaluated Tasks
Three delicate contact tasks were selected where excessive or misplaced force with a rigid robot would break or push away target objects:
- **Switch flipping**: Contacting and flipping a toggle switch using the fingertip.
- **Egg carton opening**: Detecting carton edges via touch to slide the finger under the rim and lift the lid open.
- **Card pulling**: Extracting only the frontmost card upward from a deck in a stand using compliant, controlled friction.

### Policy Learning and Baselines
For each task, 10 real demonstrations were manually collected and bootstrapped to 100 demonstrations in simulation using CEM-MPC. Policies were trained via Behavior Cloning (BC) to output 3D end-effector displacements and pneumatic pressure commands. Baselines included training on the 10 real demos alone (Real), standard data augmentation (N-Aug), 20 real demos (Real-20), a model without tactile inputs (No-Tac), and reinforcement learning in simulation using PPO.

captions.F5: Three delicate contact tasks evaluated on real hardware. From left to right: toggle switch flipping, finding thin edges to open an egg carton lid, and sliding out only the frontmost card without slippage. All tasks inherently require soft pneumatic finger compliance and tactile feedback.

sections.heading: Tremendous Acceleration and Task Success Outperforming Doubled Real Data
sections.summary: Surrogate models sped up tactile rendering by roughly 3000x while keeping fingertip position error under 4% of robot length. In real tasks, simulation augmentation (Sim+Real) outperformed all baselines, proving that simulation effectively remedies coverage shortages in small real datasets.
sections.details:
Experimental outcomes showed compelling metrics across modeling fidelity, surrogate computational efficiency, and real-world task performance.

### Real-to-Sim Modeling Accuracy
Image-based identification yielded physically sound estimates, such as Young's modulus $E_s = 0.945$ MPa and Poisson's ratio $\nu_s = 0.460$. Tip tracking error under unseen pressure inputs was $4.2 \pm 0.4$ mm on the finger (less than 4% of its >100 mm length) and $4.9 \pm 1.0$ mm on the 3-chamber arm (4.2% of length). Renderings of the back of the finger, unobserved during training, closely matched real camera views. For tactile image synthesis, PneuTac outperformed baselines like Taxim and DOT-Sim across RMSE, PSNR, and NCC metrics, realistically capturing red-to-green LED shifts upon contact.

### Massive Acceleration via Surrogate Models
Replacing full MPM calculations with surrogate networks provided enormous performance gains. Combining the kinematic model with residual torque predictions maintained joint position errors at just $0.051^\circ$ while delivering a 5x speedup (from ~50 ms to ~10 ms). Even more dramatic was tactile simulation: shifting from dense MPM particle evaluation (~60k particles) to the probe-grid plus UNet mapping dropped runtimes from ~150 s down to ~50 ms per frame—an approximately 3000x speedup. The mean indentation depth error was only $0.077$ mm across a 1.4 mm average indentation.

### Contact-Rich Real Manipulation Performance
In real robot evaluations, the $\pi_{\mathrm{Sim+Real}}$ policy pretrained on simulation-augmented demos achieved dramatic success rate improvements over using 10 real demonstrations alone (Real). Remarkably, it also outperformed the "Real-20" baseline trained on twice as many real demonstrations. While performance was matched on switch flipping, $\pi_{\mathrm{Sim+Real}}$ clearly pulled ahead on egg carton opening and card pulling, which demand more delicate control and have broader solution spaces. Exploring diverse contact variations in simulation successfully covered regions that limited real demonstrations could not reach. The substantial drop in performance for No-Tac confirmed the critical role of tactile feedback.

With only a single image for calibration, the model accurately reproduces internal LED color gradients shifting from red to green under contact indentation.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Directions
sections.summary: PneuTac unifies pneumatic soft robots and vision-based tactile sensors in simulation using MPM and 3DGS, enabling successful real-world transfer. Fast, accurate, and requiring minimal calibration data, it provides a solid foundation for tactile learning on compliant hardware.
sections.details:
This paper presented "PneuTac", an innovative framework that jointly models soft pneumatic robots and vision-based tactile sensors within a unified simulation environment.

By uniting MPM for large-deformation contact mechanics with 3DGS for fast, photorealistic appearance and tactile rendering, highly faithful digital twins can be built from only a handful of camera images. Furthermore, surrogate networks modeling residual torques and deformation mappings provide up to 3000x acceleration, while tactile-guided demonstration augmentation substantially enhances policy success rates in delicate real-world contact tasks.

Tactile manipulation with soft robots has long been hampered by fragile hardware, costly data collection, and simulator limitations. PneuTac introduces a highly practical and generalizable pathway forward.

takeaways: Directly coupling 3DGS rendering primitives to MPM particle positions is highly effective not just for overall robot bending, but also for simulating micro-scale gel deformations and optical lighting variations inside tactile sensors.

Instead of directly applying full physics simulation to policy learning or demo generation, using a surrogate pipeline (simplified model + residual neural network) achieves a 3000x speedup while preserving accuracy.
Incorporating tactile contact area progression alongside end-effector tracking into simulation control costs generates high-quality, realistic demonstrations well suited for contact-rich tasks.
limitations: Accurately capturing complex inter-object contact dynamics, such as sliding friction between stacked playing cards, remains challenging and can induce sim-to-real gaps during free exploration like PPO reinforcement learning.

Because chamber bending is approximated with a rigid multi-joint spine, fidelity under more complex deformation modes—such as torsional twisting or localized buckling from high external forces—warrants further study.
Calibration is currently performed using static equilibrium images, leaving dynamic viscoelastic behaviors and pneumatic delays during high-speed air inflation and deflation as future challenges.
